items.bodyEn: Kanagawa's inns and teahouses lined a hill road above the sea; Hiroshige's print 'View from the Hill' shows them perched over the water. The 1854 treaty that opened Japan bears the town's name. When a treaty port was due here in 1859, the shogunate opened the village of Yokohama across the inlet instead, keeping foreign traders off the Tōkaidō.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō 1833–34: Kanagawa View from the Hill; Kanagawa Treaty

items.bodyEn: Tokyo Japanese tells words apart by where the pitch drops, not by stress. はし that starts high and drops after は is 箸, chopsticks. はし that rises on し and drops on the following particle (はしが) is 橋, bridge. はし that rises and never drops is 端, edge. You left Nihonbashi over the second one.

Katakana was stretched to hold foreign sounds: a small vowel after a kana makes ティ (ti), ファ (fa), ウィ (wi). The 1991 Cabinet notice on writing loanwords lists these pairs and admits ヴ for v, while allowing the バ row instead: ヴァイオリン or バイオリン, both correct. In speech both usually come out as b.
items.sourceNote: Cabinet Notification 'Gairaigo no hyōki' (1991), Tables 1–2 and notes

items.bodyEn: 神 joins 示, an altar with offerings laid on it, to 申, which began as a drawing of forked lightning. The Shuowen Jiezi (c. 100 CE) defines it as the heavenly spirit that draws out all things. Lightning over the altar: a god, かみ. Read シン or ジン in compounds, as in 神社 (じんじゃ), shrine.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (c. 100 CE), entry 神 '天神引出萬物者也'; 申 as lightning: Kanjigen
